narrative: The model estimates a 54% chance that you will leave your job. That is only slightly above a coin flip: leaving is considered a little more likely than staying, not certain. That forecast did not use your gender, age, or health issues. Because promotion decisions here are tied to this forecast, the model’s concern is retention risk. The strongest factor in your case was your overall years of experience, which actually worked in favor of staying; with one to five years of experience, you sit in the same broad range as about half of employees predicted to stay. The second most influential factor was that you have other job opportunities while employed, and this pushed the forecast toward leaving; among employees predicted to stay, only about one in four had such options. Your industry sector was third in influence and also pushed slightly toward leaving, though an “other” sector is not unusual among stayers. Overall, your experience counted as a stabilizing signal, but outside opportunities and the sector signal were enough to tip the estimate just past half. Before treating this as a reason to deny promotion, you and your organization should consider a retention conversation that tests whether a clearer career path, recognition, or support could reduce your intent to leave. You should also discuss what would make staying worthwhile and address any dissatisfaction or exhaustion.
